docs.title: SweetPea Starter
docs.text:
An AI assistant for designing experiments with SweetPea.

You say what you want to find out. The assistant states the hypothesis, suggests a paradigm, proposes a design, and counts what the design leaves unequal between the conditions you compare. Where a choice has a cost, it puts the options to you.

docs.title: What it is built on
docs.text:
The SweetPea project. 100 published papers, re-analysed with the trial order taken into account: 11 flips and many shifts. The assistant learned from these which side effects a design can have, and its worked examples come from them.

The psyche project. A database of published experiments with open trial-level data: 1,544 experiments from 790 studies. The assistant uses it to suggest which paradigm fits a research question and what such studies compare.

SweetPea itself. It turns a description of an experiment (its factors, what must be balanced, what must not happen) into trial sequences that satisfy it.

docs.title: Teaching examples
docs.text:
One experiment each, walked through with pictures: what is compared, what the design leaves unequal, and what can be done about it.

  1. Masked number priming: a side effect of crossing two stimuli from the same set.
  2. The trial before: a side effect of shuffling in small sets.
  3. Two things in one place: no design without a cost, only a choice between costs.

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text: One Stroop experiment grown in four questions, with an assistant or as notebooks: start here.

docs.title: Example library
docs.text:
Experiments described in one fixed format, from the research question to the design. These pages are generated from the examples that the assistant reads (skills/sweetpea/examples/).

Example Paradigm Takeaway A distractor that is usually in one place additional singleton search Often there is no design without a cost, only a choice between costs, and which cost is acceptable depends on the analysis. Ask which comparisons are planned before proposing a design. Lay out the options with what each keeps and gives up, say which fits the planned comparisons and why, and write the chosen design down so that design and analysis agree. Masked number priming masked priming A complete crossing of two stimuli from the same set contains the pairs with the same item twice, and those can only be congruent. When you remove them, check what the first stimulus then says about the second: the second must be equally expected in every compared condition. Simon task: the trial before Simon task with a prime word Making things even within a short stretch of trials (sets, mini-blocks) changes what follows what: a trial then follows its own type, its side and its response less often than half of the time, and this does not even out over a block. When a user asks for such sets, say so, and offer to make what repeats from the trial before part of the design. The sets can stay.

docs.title: A distractor that is usually in one place
docs.text:
Source: Gong & Theeuwes (2021), Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, Experiment 3. doi:10.3758/s13414-020-02142-8

Takeaway. Often there is no design without a cost, only a choice between costs, and which cost is acceptable depends on the analysis. Ask which comparisons are planned before proposing a design. When two things cannot share a level (a place, an item, a key), the level that one of them occupies most cannot also be an ordinary level for the other. Lay out the options with what each keeps and gives up, say which fits the planned comparisons and why, and write the chosen design down so that design and analysis agree.

docs.title: Research question
docs.text:
What, and why. Attentional control: people learn where a salient distractor tends to appear and suppress that location. Is the suppression of a location fixed, or does it adjust to how salient the distractor on the current trial is?

How. Visual search for a diamond among eight shapes. On most trials another shape stands out too (the distractor), weakly or strongly, most often at one location. Suppression is read from how much a distractor slows the search at its frequent location, compared with other locations and with no distractor.

Part used. A distractor at the frequent location against no distractor.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: Response time with the distractor at its usual place against response time without a distractor, within participants.

docs.title: Design as published
docs.text: Decision Chosen Reason given What follows Distractor Absent on 1 trial in 6; otherwise at one place on 65% of the trials, at each of the 7 others on 5% The manipulation: people are to learn the place Unequal on purpose Target without a distractor Equally often at each of the 8 places Stated At the distractor's usual place on 1 trial in 8 Target with a distractor At random among the 7 places the distractor does not occupy Stated With the distractor at its usual place, never at that place

docs.title: What to balance
docs.text:
Assumption. Trials with the distractor at its usual place and trials without a distractor differ only in the distractor.

Where it fails. They differ in where the target can be. The target is at the distractor's usual place on 1 trial in 8 without a distractor, on 1 in 7 with the distractor elsewhere, and never with the distractor at that place.

Those trials are in the design on purpose: the paper compares targets at that place with targets elsewhere, to show that the place is suppressed, and finds them slower. The problem is not that they exist. It is that the comparison with "no distractor" counts them as ordinary baseline trials. This is a mismatch between design and analysis, not an accident of the design.

This is a regular factor (the place of the target), not a derived one. It is the simplest case of a combination that cannot exist.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Three wishes cannot all hold: the distractor is usually at one place (the manipulation); target and distractor are never at the same place; and where the target is tells nothing and is told by nothing. The options differ in how often the target is at the distractor's usual place (design(choice) in design.py). Each keeps one wish and gives up two.

Choice Target at the usual place Keeps Gives up "as often" as at any other free place (the published design) 1 trial in 8 without a distractor, 1 in 7 with the distractor elsewhere; 9% of all trials A distractor elsewhere says nothing about the target The usual place holds the target less often than the other places; 1 baseline trial in 8 has its target where the compared condition never has it "never" never Every trial has the target elsewhere, so the baseline can use all its trials A place that never holds the target can be learned as such; no trial is left to compare targets there with targets elsewhere "more often", only on trials with the distractor at another place 1 in 8 without a distractor, as in the original; more with the distractor elsewhere (twice as often in the code; 10 to 7 gives exactly 1 in 8 over all trials) Every place holds the target equally often; the baseline is as in the original With a distractor elsewhere, the target is likelier at the usual place than anywhere else

The third option leaves the trials without a distractor alone, because they are the baseline of the main comparison. In SweetPea it is a second copy of some trials: a factor copy in the crossing, and an Exclude of every second copy except those with the target at the usual place and the distractor elsewhere.

docs.title: Which design for which analysis
docs.text:
No option is best in general. Which fits depends on the comparisons that are planned (best_for(comparisons) in design.py). This is reasoning from the counts, not a result of the paper.

Planned comparison What it needs Fits Why Distractor at its usual place against no distractor The same target places in both "never", or any option with the baseline formed from the trials with the target elsewhere With the distractor at its usual place the target is always elsewhere Distractor at its usual place against distractor at another place The same "never", or the others restricted to the target elsewhere; "more often" leaves fewest usable trials Trials with the distractor elsewhere can have the target at the usual place Target at the usual place against target elsewhere, without a distractor Trials with the target at the usual place "as often"; "more often" if targets being rare at that place is itself a worry "never" has no such trials

So: if only the first two are planned, "never" uses every trial, at the price of a place that never holds the target. If the third is planned, as in the paper, "never" is out, and the baseline of the other comparisons has to leave out the trials with the target at the usual place.

In every option the trials with the distractor at its usual place have the target at the seven other places. A baseline that is fair to them is made of trials that have the target at those seven places: target_place == "elsewhere".

docs.title: What to present
docs.text:
Ask first which comparisons are planned. Then show all three options with the tables above, say which fits those comparisons and why, and name what it gives up. Do not present one as correct in general. Write the chosen design down with target_place as a factor, so that the choice is explicit and the analysis can follow it.

Counts of one generated block of each (simplified frequencies), as target elsewhere / target at the usual place:

distractor as often never more often none 7 / 1 7 / 0 7 / 1 at its usual place 28 / 0 28 / 0 28 / 0 at another place 42 / 7 42 / 0 42 / 14

docs.title: Masked number priming
docs.text:
Source: Zerweck et al. (2021), Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, Experiment 3. doi:10.3758/s13414-021-02312-2

Takeaway. A complete crossing of two stimuli from the same set contains the pairs with the same item twice, and those can only be congruent. When you remove them, check what the first stimulus then says about the second: the second must be equally expected in every compared condition.

docs.title: Research question
docs.text:
What, and why. Unconscious processing: is the magnitude of a number processed when the number is masked and cannot be reported? The paper tests the standard evidence for this by comparing a direct and an indirect measure of the masked number.

How. Masked priming: a masked number (the prime) precedes a visible one (the target), which is classified as smaller or larger than five. If the prime's magnitude was processed, responses are faster when both fall on the same side of five (the priming effect).

Part used. The priming effect in the indirect task.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: Response time on congruent against incongruent trials, within participants.

docs.title: Design as published
docs.text:
Decision Chosen Reason given What follows Numbers 1, 4, 6, 9, as digit or word Replicates Dehaene et al. (1998) Two numbers on each side of five Primes and targets Same four numbers Same A prime can equal its target Pairs All 16 number pairs x 4 notation combinations, once per block (64 trials) None Half congruent; a quarter show the same number twice Order Random per block None The previous trial is not controlled

The design is counterbalanced, not only randomised: prime and target are completely crossed. The same-number trials are cells of that crossing, so they are a consequence of the counterbalancing and not an accident of sampling.

docs.title: What to balance
docs.text:
Assumption. Congruent and incongruent trials differ only in whether prime and target share the category.

Where it fails. Half of the congruent trials repeat the number; no incongruent trial can.

different number same number congruent 16 16 incongruent 32 0

A congruent response may be faster because the number repeats, not because the category matches. Reordering trials cannot change this: an incongruent pair with the same number does not exist.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
In the design (functions in design.py):

Option Same-number pairs Congruent share Trials per congruent : incongruent pair Cost proposed: each prime has one congruent and one fixed incongruent target none 1/2 8 : 8 Half of the incongruent pairs are not shown to a participant; use two mappings across participants. Two targets per prime, each expected at 50%. drop_identical_double_congruent none 1/2 8 : 4 After a prime, its congruent target is twice as likely as each incongruent target (50% against 25%), so congruent targets are the expected numbers. Congruency itself and the response stay at one half. drop_identical_only none 1/3 4 : 4 Incongruent trials are twice as frequent as congruent ones; 48 trials. separate_number_sets: primes 1, 4, 6, 9, targets 2, 3, 7, 8 none 1/2 4 : 4 Primes never occur as targets, which is a different question (priming by numbers never responded to).

In the analysis, with the published design:

Option Cost Leave the same-number trials out of the congruent mean Congruent mean from 16 trials per block, incongruent from 32. Participants still saw the repetitions. Three trial types: same number, congruent with different numbers, incongruent Same trial counts. Identity cannot be crossed with congruency, because one of the four cells does not exist.

Unequal in every option. Numerical distance: congruent pairs of different numbers are 3 apart, incongruent pairs 2, 5 or 8 (5 in proposed).

None of the options is the correct one; which to take depends on the claim.

docs.title: Design to propose
docs.text:
proposed(). Raise number identity with the user, show this design, and name the alternatives with their costs.

Prime and target stay separate factors, crossed as prime x congruency. Two constraints remove what must not occur: Exclude the trials with the same number, and Exclude the incongruent pairs outside the mapping.

When checking any option, state what the prime predicts separately for the trial type, the response and the target number. In drop_identical_double_congruent the first two stay at one half and only the third is unequal.

as_published proposed trials 64 64 congruent / incongruent 32 / 32 32 / 32 congruent trials with the same number 16 0 trials per pair, congruent : incongruent 4 : 4 8 : 8 targets that can follow a prime 4 2 how expected the target is after its prime, congruent : incongruent 25% : 25% 50% : 50%

docs.title: Simon task: the trial before
docs.text:
Source: Dunaway & Weissman (2026), Psychological Research, Experiment 4. doi:10.1007/s00426-025-02216-y

Takeaway. Making things even within a short stretch of trials (sets, mini-blocks) changes what follows what: a trial then follows its own type, its side and its response less often than half of the time, and this does not even out over a block. When a user asks for such sets, say so, and offer to make what repeats from the trial before part of the design. The sets can stay.

docs.title: Research question
docs.text:
What, and why. Cognitive control: when two irrelevant signals are present at once, do their effects on a response add up or interact? The answer speaks to whether one control process handles all distraction or several handle different kinds.

How. A prime word (Red, Green or Cross) is followed by a red or green square on the left or right. Participants press the key of the colour. The word can match the colour or not; the side can match the side of the key or not (the Simon effect). The two effects are compared across their combinations.

Part used. The Simon effect and its interaction with prime compatibility.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: Response time and errors by prime compatibility (compatible, neutral, incompatible) and Simon congruency (congruent, incongruent), within participants.

docs.title: Design as published
docs.text:
Decision Chosen Reason given What follows Combinations 3 words x 2 sides x 2 colours = 12 Fully crossed design Each of the 6 conditions twice per set Sets A block is 9 sets of the 12 combinations, each set in its own random order "By presenting each of the 12 possible combinations equally often, we avoided contingency learning confounds." Inside a set a trial follows its own type less often than another type Trial before Not controlled None A congruent trial follows a congruent one in 46% of cases (11/24), not 50%

The design is counterbalanced for the combinations, by choice and for a stated reason. The trial before is a side effect of that choice.

docs.title: What to balance
docs.text:
Assumption. The compared conditions have the same kinds of trial before them. Congruency effects depend on the trial before (the congruency sequence effect), and so do repetitions of the side and of the response.

Where it fails. Inside a set, whatever was just shown is scarcer among the trials that are left. Between two sets nothing is biased. The borders are fair, and fair cannot make up for the bias inside the sets, so it does not even out over a block. It concerns every property that is even within a set, derived or not.

What repeats from one trial to the next, over many blocks of shuffled sets:

Set size Trial type Side Response The same square 2 (one congruent, one incongruent square) 25% 50% 50% 12.5% 4 (each square once) 37.5% 37.5% 37.5% 6.25% 12 (the original) 45.8% 45.8% 45.8% 18.75% without sets 50% 50% 50% 25%

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
In the design (functions in design.py):

Option Sets kept What repeats Cost proposed: sets of 12, merged with a block that crosses "the side repeats" with "the colour repeats" over the whole block yes trial type 50%, side 50%, response 50%, same square 25% One extra trial per block (109). Inside a set the transitions stay free. About four minutes to generate at 109 trials, seconds at 49. within_every_four: the same, and also even within every four trials yes the same Stricter than needed: a regularity in the order. Seconds with CMSGen. conditions_crossed: each of the 6 conditions follows each 3 times yes trial type 50% About two minutes; side and response are not addressed. trial_type_only: Simon congruency crossed with that of the trial before yes trial type 50%, side and response further from 50% than before Evens out one property by adding trials on which side and colour both change. Do not propose. No sets: cross the square with the square before no all even Gives up the sets and what they were for.

In the analysis, with the published design:

Option Cost Add the trial before as a factor of the analysis More cells with fewer trials each; the first trial of a block drops out. Reweight the conditions to the same share of each kind of trial before Changes what the condition mean estimates; needs a choice of weights.

What smaller sets cost. Sets and an even trial before are two demands on the same order. With sets of 12 no further restriction was found. With sets of 4 (each square once) every set has to start with the square that ended the last one, because a square can repeat only across a border. With sets of 2 the order of trial types is fixed (c i i c c i i c). Say this when a user wants small sets.

None of the options is the correct one; which to take depends on the claim.

docs.title: What to tell the user
docs.text:
When someone asks for sets, mini-blocks or "each condition once every n trials", say these four things before writing the design:

  1. Sets make every combination equally frequent and evenly spread. They also make a trial follow its own type less often than half of the time, and that does not even out over a block. Give the number for their set size.
  2. It concerns everything that is even within a set: the trial type, the side, the response, the stimulus itself.
  3. It matters when the measure depends on the trial before, which is usual in conflict, switching and priming tasks. Ask whether it does.
  4. It can be made part of the design with the sets kept. Evening out one property alone makes the others worse, so balance all of them, and say what small sets cost.

docs.title: Design to propose
docs.text:
proposed(). Raise what repeats from the trial before with the user, show this design, and name the alternatives with their costs.

Two blocks, merged with Merge. The first holds the twelve combinations in repeat mode: once in every set. The second crosses "the side repeats" with "the colour repeats" in weight mode: each of the four cases equally often, anywhere in the block. Nothing is counted by hand; the two blocks say what is even where. Inside a set the combinations are even and the transitions are free; over the block the transitions are even. The balance is over all trials, not within each of the six compared conditions; conditions_crossed does that.

as_published proposed trials per block 108 109 sets of 12 with every combination once 9 9 the same trial type follows 45.8% in the long run 50% in every block the side repeats, the response repeats 45.8% 50% the same square repeats 18.75% 25%

as_published() gives a valid block of shuffled sets, but SweetPea's sampler does not draw orders the way a shuffle does. The rates above are exact under shuffling, not counts from that block.

docs.title: Two things in one place
docs.text:
Does a distractor still disturb us at a place where we have learned to expect it?

Based on Gong & Theeuwes (2021), Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, Experiment 3. doi:10.3758/s13414-020-02142-8

docs.title: The task and the question
docs.text: Scroll, or use the buttons under each block.

docs.title: Three designs
docs.text: Each design keeps one of the three and gives up two. None is the right one.

docs.title: What is simplified
docs.text: The original has two kinds of distractor and two groups, and its distractor is at the usual place on 65% of the trials that have one. Here there is one kind, four times as often at its usual place as at any other single place.

docs.title: In SweetPea
docs.text:
One design, with the choice as its argument.

import pandas as pd
from sweetpea import (Factor, Level, DerivedLevel, WithinTrial, Exclude,
                      CrossBlock, synthesize_trials, CMSGen)

places = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6", "7", "8"]
usual = "1"                                  # the place where the distractor usually is


def design(target_at_usual_place):
    """One block. `target_at_usual_place` is "as often", "never" or "more often":
    how often the target is at the distractor's usual place, compared with any other free place."""
    target = Factor("target", places)

    # The distractor: absent, or at a place; four times as often at its usual place as at any other.
    distractor = Factor("distractor", [Level("none", 1), Level(usual, 4)]
                                      + [Level(p, 1) for p in places if p != usual])

    # Two things cannot be in the same place.
    def same_place(target, distractor):
        return target == distractor

    def different_places(target, distractor):
        return target != distractor

    overlap = Factor("overlap", [
        DerivedLevel("same place", WithinTrial(same_place, [target, distractor])),
        DerivedLevel("different places", WithinTrial(different_places, [target, distractor])),
    ])

    # Where the target is, by name, so that it can be counted and kept apart.
    def at_usual_place(target):
        return target == usual

    def elsewhere(target):
        return target != usual

    target_place = Factor("target_place", [
        DerivedLevel("usual place", WithinTrial(at_usual_place, [target])),
        DerivedLevel("elsewhere", WithinTrial(elsewhere, [target])),
    ])

    factors = [target, distractor, overlap, target_place]
    crossing = [target, distractor]
    constraints = [Exclude((overlap, "same place"))]

    if target_at_usual_place == "never":
        constraints.append(Exclude((target_place, "usual place")))

    if target_at_usual_place == "more often":
        # A second copy of some trials: those with the target at the usual place while the distractor
        # is at another place. Trials without a distractor are the baseline and get no second copy.
        copy = Factor("copy", ["first", "second"])

        def unwanted(copy, target, distractor):
            doubled = target == usual and distractor not in ("none", usual)
            return copy == "second" and not doubled

        def wanted(copy, target, distractor):
            return not unwanted(copy, target, distractor)

        second_copy = Factor("second_copy", [
            DerivedLevel("unwanted", WithinTrial(unwanted, [copy, target, distractor])),
            DerivedLevel("wanted", WithinTrial(wanted, [copy, target, distractor])),
        ])
        factors += [copy, second_copy]
        crossing = [target, distractor, copy]
        constraints.append(Exclude((second_copy, "unwanted")))

    return CrossBlock(design=factors, crossing=crossing, constraints=constraints,
                      require_complete_crossing=False)


for choice in ["as often", "never", "more often"]:
    trials = pd.DataFrame(synthesize_trials(design(choice), 1, CMSGen)[0])
    kind = trials["distractor"].map(lambda d: "none" if d == "none" else "usual place" if d == usual else "another place")
    print(choice, len(trials), "trials")
    print(pd.crosstab(kind, trials["target_place"]))

Trials per block, as target elsewhere / target at the usual place:

distractor as often (85 trials) never (77) more often (92) none 7 / 1 7 / 0 7 / 1 at its usual place 28 / 0 28 / 0 28 / 0 at another place 42 / 7 42 / 0 42 / 14

In the code, "more often" is twice as often, which keeps the block short. The picture uses 10 to 7, which spreads the target evenly over all places.

docs.title: The point
docs.text:
• Often there is no design without a cost, only a choice between costs.
  • A design that is not written down still makes that choice, unseen.
  • Written as a specification, the choice is explicit and can be counted, and the analysis can be made to agree with it.

docs.title: Masked number priming
docs.text:
Is the meaning of a number processed when the number cannot be seen?

Based on Zerweck et al. (2021), Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, Experiment 3. doi:10.3758/s13414-021-02312-2

docs.title: The task and the question
docs.text: Scroll, or use the buttons under each block.

docs.title: From the published design to a better one
docs.text: Nobody decided that half of the congruent trials repeat the number. It follows from two choices: the same four numbers for primes and targets, and every pair equally often.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
• A participant never sees half of the incongruent pairs. A second mapping for the other half of the participants covers them.
  • Congruent pairs stay 3 apart and incongruent pairs 5. These four numbers allow nothing else.

docs.title: In SweetPea
docs.text:
Prime and target are the factors. Two constraints say what must not occur.

from sweetpea import (Factor, DerivedLevel, WithinTrial, Exclude, MinimumTrials,
                      CrossBlock, synthesize_trials, CMSGen)

numbers = ["1", "4", "6", "9"]
prime = Factor("prime", numbers)
target = Factor("target", numbers)

# Congruency: are prime and target on the same side of five?
def same_side(prime, target):
    return (int(prime) < 5) == (int(target) < 5)

def opposite_sides(prime, target):
    return not same_side(prime, target)

congruency = Factor("congruency", [
    DerivedLevel("congruent", WithinTrial(same_side, [prime, target])),
    DerivedLevel("incongruent", WithinTrial(opposite_sides, [prime, target])),
])

# Repetition: is the prime the same number as the target?
def same_number(prime, target):
    return prime == target

def different_number(prime, target):
    return prime != target

repetition = Factor("repetition", [
    DerivedLevel("repeated", WithinTrial(same_number, [prime, target])),
    DerivedLevel("different", WithinTrial(different_number, [prime, target])),
])

# Every prime has one fixed incongruent target; the other incongruent pair is left out.
partner = {"1": "6", "4": "9", "6": "1", "9": "4"}

def left_out(prime, target):
    return opposite_sides(prime, target) and partner[prime] != target

def kept(prime, target):
    return not left_out(prime, target)

pairing = Factor("pairing", [
    DerivedLevel("left out", WithinTrial(left_out, [prime, target])),
    DerivedLevel("kept", WithinTrial(kept, [prime, target])),
])

block = CrossBlock(
    design=[prime, target, congruency, repetition, pairing],
    crossing=[prime, congruency],          # every prime equally often congruent and incongruent
    constraints=[
        Exclude((repetition, "repeated")),  # no trial shows the same number twice
        Exclude((pairing, "left out")),     # one incongruent target per prime
        MinimumTrials(64),
    ],
)
trials = synthesize_trials(block, 1, CMSGen)[0]

The generated block: 64 trials, 32 congruent, each of the eight pairs 8 times. The original also showed each number as a digit or a word; that is left out.

docs.title: The point
docs.text:
• A few explicit choices specified the design. What mattered was a consequence nobody stated.
  • Written as a specification and counted, such consequences show before any data are collected.

docs.title: The trial before
docs.text:
If every trial type is shown equally often, does it matter what came before?

Based on Dunaway & Weissman (2026), Psychological Research, Experiment 4. doi:10.1007/s00426-025-02216-y

docs.title: The task and the question
docs.text: Scroll, or use the buttons under each block.

docs.title: From the original design to a better one
docs.text:
The original shuffles its trials in sets of twelve. Smaller sets show the same thing more strongly.

Nobody decided that a trial should follow its own type less often. It follows from shuffling small sets. The side of the square, the response and the square itself are affected in the same way, and the design balances those too.

docs.title: What is simplified
docs.text: The original shows a word before the square, which gives twelve combinations per set. The page leaves the word out. Sets of four and of two are not in the original.

docs.title: In SweetPea
docs.text:
The code for the sets chosen above.

A set is one congruent and one incongruent square. Two blocks, merged. The first keeps the sets. The second crosses what repeats from the trial before over the whole block. So inside a set congruency is even and the transitions are free; over the block the transitions are even.

from sweetpea import (Factor, DerivedLevel, WithinTrial, Transition, MinimumTrials,
                      MultiCrossBlock, Merge, RepeatMode, AlignmentMode, synthesize_trials, CMSGen)

side = Factor("side", ["left", "right"])
colour = Factor("colour", ["red", "green"])

# Congruency: does the square appear on the side of its key?
key = {"red": "left", "green": "right"}

def on_key_side(side, colour):
    return key[colour] == side

def on_other_side(side, colour):
    return key[colour] != side

congruency = Factor("congruency", [
    DerivedLevel("congruent", WithinTrial(on_key_side, [side, colour])),
    DerivedLevel("incongruent", WithinTrial(on_other_side, [side, colour])),
])

# Does the side repeat from the trial before? Does the colour?  [0] is this trial, [-1] the one before.
def repeats(factor):
    return factor[0] == factor[-1]

def changes(factor):
    return factor[0] != factor[-1]

side_repeats = Factor("side_repeats", [
    DerivedLevel("repeats", Transition(repeats, [side])),
    DerivedLevel("changes", Transition(changes, [side])),
])
colour_repeats = Factor("colour_repeats", [
    DerivedLevel("repeats", Transition(repeats, [colour])),
    DerivedLevel("changes", Transition(changes, [colour])),
])

# The sets: one congruent and one incongruent square in every two trials.
sets = MultiCrossBlock(design=[side, colour, congruency], crossings=[[congruency]],
                       constraints=[MinimumTrials(32)],
                       mode=RepeatMode.REPEAT,                  # once in every set
                       alignment=AlignmentMode.PARALLEL_START)

# The transitions: side repeats or not, crossed with colour repeats or not, over the whole block.
transitions = MultiCrossBlock(design=[side, colour, side_repeats, colour_repeats],
                              crossings=[[side_repeats, colour_repeats]],
                              constraints=[MinimumTrials(33)],          # one more: the first trial has no trial before
                              mode=RepeatMode.WEIGHT,           # equally often, anywhere in the block
                              alignment=AlignmentMode.PARALLEL_START)

# Both at once.
block = Merge([sets, transitions], alignment=AlignmentMode.PARALLEL_START)
trials = synthesize_trials(block, 1, CMSGen)[0]

The generated block: 33 trials, every set intact; trial type, side and response each repeat on half of the trials, the same square on a quarter.

A set is each of the four squares once. Two blocks, merged. The first keeps the sets. The second crosses what repeats from the trial before over the whole block. So inside a set the squares are even and the transitions are free; over the block the transitions are even.

from sweetpea import (Factor, DerivedLevel, Transition, MinimumTrials,
                      MultiCrossBlock, Merge, RepeatMode, AlignmentMode, synthesize_trials, CMSGen)

side = Factor("side", ["left", "right"])
colour = Factor("colour", ["red", "green"])

# Does the side repeat from the trial before? Does the colour?  [0] is this trial, [-1] the one before.
def repeats(factor):
    return factor[0] == factor[-1]

def changes(factor):
    return factor[0] != factor[-1]

side_repeats = Factor("side_repeats", [
    DerivedLevel("repeats", Transition(repeats, [side])),
    DerivedLevel("changes", Transition(changes, [side])),
])
colour_repeats = Factor("colour_repeats", [
    DerivedLevel("repeats", Transition(repeats, [colour])),
    DerivedLevel("changes", Transition(changes, [colour])),
])

# The sets: each of the four squares once in every four trials.
sets = MultiCrossBlock(design=[side, colour], crossings=[[side, colour]],
                       constraints=[MinimumTrials(32)],
                       mode=RepeatMode.REPEAT,                  # once in every set
                       alignment=AlignmentMode.PARALLEL_START)

# The transitions: side repeats or not, crossed with colour repeats or not, over the whole block.
transitions = MultiCrossBlock(design=[side, colour, side_repeats, colour_repeats],
                              crossings=[[side_repeats, colour_repeats]],
                              constraints=[MinimumTrials(33)],          # one more: the first trial has no trial before
                              mode=RepeatMode.WEIGHT,           # equally often, anywhere in the block
                              alignment=AlignmentMode.PARALLEL_START)

# Both at once.
block = Merge([sets, transitions], alignment=AlignmentMode.PARALLEL_START)
trials = synthesize_trials(block, 1, CMSGen)[0]

The generated block: 33 trials, every set intact; trial type, side and response each repeat on half of the trials, the same square on a quarter.

A set is the twelve combinations, each once. Two blocks, merged. The first keeps the sets. The second crosses what repeats from the trial before over the whole block. So inside a set the combinations are even and the transitions are free; over the block the transitions are even.

from sweetpea import (Factor, DerivedLevel, Transition, MinimumTrials,
                      MultiCrossBlock, Merge, RepeatMode, AlignmentMode, synthesize_trials, CMSGen)

word = Factor("word", ["red", "green", "cross"])    # the word shown before the square
side = Factor("side", ["left", "right"])
colour = Factor("colour", ["red", "green"])

# Does the side repeat from the trial before? Does the colour?  [0] is this trial, [-1] the one before.
def repeats(factor):
    return factor[0] == factor[-1]

def changes(factor):
    return factor[0] != factor[-1]

side_repeats = Factor("side_repeats", [
    DerivedLevel("repeats", Transition(repeats, [side])),
    DerivedLevel("changes", Transition(changes, [side])),
])
colour_repeats = Factor("colour_repeats", [
    DerivedLevel("repeats", Transition(repeats, [colour])),
    DerivedLevel("changes", Transition(changes, [colour])),
])

# The sets: each of the twelve combinations once in every twelve trials.
sets = MultiCrossBlock(design=[word, side, colour], crossings=[[word, side, colour]],
                       constraints=[MinimumTrials(48)],
                       mode=RepeatMode.REPEAT,                  # once in every set
                       alignment=AlignmentMode.PARALLEL_START)

# The transitions: side repeats or not, crossed with colour repeats or not, over the whole block.
transitions = MultiCrossBlock(design=[side, colour, side_repeats, colour_repeats],
                              crossings=[[side_repeats, colour_repeats]],
                              constraints=[MinimumTrials(49)],          # one more: the first trial has no trial before
                              mode=RepeatMode.WEIGHT,           # equally often, anywhere in the block
                              alignment=AlignmentMode.PARALLEL_START)

# Both at once.
block = Merge([sets, transitions], alignment=AlignmentMode.PARALLEL_START)
trials = synthesize_trials(block, 1, CMSGen)[0]

The generated block: 49 trials, every set intact; trial type, side and response each repeat on half of the trials, the same square on a quarter. The full block of 9 sets (109 trials) took about four minutes to generate.

docs.title: The point
docs.text:
• Making things even within a short stretch of trials changes what follows what, and it does not even out over a block.
  • What repeats from the trial before can be a factor of the design like any other. The sets can stay: inside a set the combinations are even and the transitions are free; over the whole block the transitions are even.
  • Every rule costs freedom. The smaller the sets, the less is left.

docs.title: Tutorial: four questions about one task
docs.text:
One Stroop experiment, grown in four steps. Each step is a research question. With an assistant, you say what you want to find out and it builds the design with you. Without one, each page is a notebook: the design in small pieces, a playable block of the experiment, and the count tables.

Step The question New in the design 1. Congruency Does an irrelevant word interfere? Regular factors, a derived factor, what is crossed 2. The trial before Does a conflict change how the next trial is handled? A transition factor 3. Adaptation Do people adjust to how frequent conflict is? Blocks that differ in proportion 4. Transfer Does adapting to conflict carry over to the next task? A second task, mini-blocks nested in one design

docs.title: With an assistant
docs.text: Open the repository in a Codespace, start your assistant (claude, codex or gemini), and say the line under "With your assistant" on each page, in your own words. Stuck? Say "Run the guided tutorial."

docs.title: Without one
docs.text: Every page has an "Open in Colab" button. The notebooks build on each other: step 2 keeps the block of step 1, step 3 turns its proportion into the manipulation, step 4 adds a task and nests the mini-blocks in one design.

docs.title: Step 1. Congruency
docs.text: · notebook · script

docs.title: The experiment
docs.text: A block from the design built on this page. Press play, or step through it.

docs.title: With your assistant
docs.text: I want to run a Stroop experiment to test the congruency effect. What is it about, and what do I need to decide?

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
The question. Does an irrelevant word interfere with naming a colour?

Prediction. Naming the ink is slower when the word names another colour (incongruent) than when it names the same one (congruent). The difference is the congruency effect.

The analysis. Response time on congruent trials against incongruent trials.

The decision. With three colours there are 3 congruent and 6 incongruent pairs of ink and word. Two wishes pull apart: every pair equally often (then one third of the trials is congruent) or half of the trials congruent (then the word tells something about the ink). This page builds both and counts them.

docs.title: The factors
docs.text:
A regular factor is set freely on every trial. The ink colour and the word are regular factors.

import pandas as pd
from sweetpea import (Factor, DerivedLevel, WithinTrial, Transition, Exclude, MinimumTrials,
                      CrossBlock, synthesize_trials, CMSGen)

colours = ["red", "green", "blue"]

# regular factors: set freely on every trial
colour = Factor("colour", colours)      # the ink
word = Factor("word", colours)          # what the word says

Congruency is not set freely: it follows from the colour and the word. That is a derived factor.

# a derived factor: it follows from colour and word on the same trial
def same(colour, word):
    return colour == word


def different(colour, word):
    return colour != word


congruency = Factor("congruency", [
    DerivedLevel("congruent", WithinTrial(same, [colour, word])),
    DerivedLevel("incongruent", WithinTrial(different, [colour, word])),
])

docs.title: Option A: every pair equally often
docs.text:
Colour and word are crossed, so each of the 9 pairs occurs equally often. MinimumTrials(18) asks for two rounds of the crossing.

block_a = CrossBlock(design=[colour, word, congruency], crossing=[colour, word],
                     constraints=[MinimumTrials(18)])
trials_a = pd.DataFrame(synthesize_trials(block_a, 1, CMSGen)[0])
display(pd.crosstab(trials_a["colour"], trials_a["word"]))
display(trials_a["congruency"].value_counts().to_frame("trials"))
word blue green red colour blue 2 2 2 green 2 2 2 red 2 2 2 trials congruency incongruent 12 congruent 6

docs.title: Option B: half of the trials congruent
docs.text:
Every pair once, and the congruent pairs a second time. Two helper factors do that: copy numbers the copies, and the copies that are too many are excluded. The helper is written once here and used again in steps 2 and 3.

def pairs_with_copies(congruent_copies, incongruent_copies):
    """Two helper factors that make every congruent pair occur `congruent_copies` times
    and every incongruent pair `incongruent_copies` times."""
    copy = Factor("copy", [str(n) for n in range(1, max(congruent_copies, incongruent_copies) + 1)])

    def too_many(copy, colour, word):
        return int(copy) > (congruent_copies if colour == word else incongruent_copies)

    def wanted(copy, colour, word):
        return not too_many(copy, colour, word)

    extra_copy = Factor("extra_copy", [
        DerivedLevel("too many", WithinTrial(too_many, [copy, colour, word])),
        DerivedLevel("wanted", WithinTrial(wanted, [copy, colour, word])),
    ])
    return copy, extra_copy

copy, extra_copy = pairs_with_copies(congruent_copies=2, incongruent_copies=1)
block_b = CrossBlock(design=[colour, word, congruency, copy, extra_copy],
                     crossing=[colour, word, copy],
                     constraints=[Exclude((extra_copy, "too many")), MinimumTrials(24)],
                     require_complete_crossing=False)
trials_b = pd.DataFrame(synthesize_trials(block_b, 1, CMSGen)[0])
display(pd.crosstab(trials_b["colour"], trials_b["word"]))
display(trials_b["congruency"].value_counts().to_frame("trials"))
word blue green red colour blue 4 2 2 green 2 4 2 red 2 2 4 trials congruency congruent 12 incongruent 12

docs.title: What does each option cost?
docs.text:
How often is a word shown in its own colour? One third means the word tells nothing about the ink.

cost = pd.DataFrame({
    "congruent trials (%)": [round((t["congruency"] == "congruent").mean() * 100) for t in (trials_a, trials_b)],
    "word is in its own colour (%)": [round((t["word"] == t["colour"]).mean() * 100) for t in (trials_a, trials_b)],
}, index=["A: every pair equally often", "B: half congruent"])
display(cost)
congruent trials (%) word is in its own colour (%) A: every pair equally often 33 33 B: half congruent 50 50

Check. In which option could a participant guess the ink from the word? In which are there fewer congruent trials? Neither is free: which cost is acceptable depends on what you compare.

Try. Add a fourth colour to colours and run again. What happens to the share of congruent trials in option A?

Next. Step 2 keeps option B and asks what happened on the trial before.

docs.title: Step 2. The trial before
docs.text: · notebook · script

docs.title: The experiment
docs.text: A block from the design built on this page. Press play, or step through it.

docs.title: With your assistant
docs.text: Now I want to test whether the congruency effect depends on the trial before: is it smaller right after an incongruent trial? What is the hypothesis behind that, and what does the design need?

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
So far. Step 1 gave a block with half of the trials congruent and every pair of a kind equally often. This step keeps that block and adds one factor.

The question. Does a conflict change how the next trial is handled?

Prediction (conflict adaptation). The congruency effect is smaller after an incongruent trial than after a congruent one.

The alternative to rule out. Nothing is adjusted; trials that repeat a colour or a word from the trial before are simply faster, and such repeats are spread unevenly.

The analysis. The congruency effect after a congruent trial against the congruency effect after an incongruent trial.

docs.title: As in step 1
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
from sweetpea import (Factor, DerivedLevel, WithinTrial, Transition, Exclude, MinimumTrials,
                      CrossBlock, synthesize_trials, CMSGen)

colours = ["red", "green", "blue"]

# regular factors: set freely on every trial
colour = Factor("colour", colours)      # the ink
word = Factor("word", colours)          # what the word says

# a derived factor: it follows from colour and word on the same trial
def same(colour, word):
    return colour == word


def different(colour, word):
    return colour != word


congruency = Factor("congruency", [
    DerivedLevel("congruent", WithinTrial(same, [colour, word])),
    DerivedLevel("incongruent", WithinTrial(different, [colour, word])),

def pairs_with_copies(congruent_copies, incongruent_copies):

    and every incongruent pair `incongruent_copies` times."""

    def too_many(copy, colour, word):
        return int(copy) > (congruent_copies if colour == word else incongruent_copies)

    def wanted(copy, colour, word):

docs.title: New: the trial before as a factor
docs.text:
A transition factor follows from the trial before: [0] is this trial, [-1] the one before.

def after_congruent(colour, word):
    return colour[-1] == word[-1]


def after_incongruent(colour, word):
    return colour[-1] != word[-1]


trial_before = Factor("trial_before", [
    DerivedLevel("congruent", Transition(after_congruent, [colour, word])),
    DerivedLevel("incongruent", Transition(after_incongruent, [colour, word])),
])

docs.title: The block
docs.text:
The block of step 1, crossed with the trial before: 12 trials times 2 is 24, plus a first trial, which has no trial before.

copy, extra_copy = pairs_with_copies(congruent_copies=2, incongruent_copies=1)
block = CrossBlock(design=[colour, word, congruency, copy, extra_copy, trial_before],
                   crossing=[colour, word, copy, trial_before],
                   constraints=[Exclude((extra_copy, "too many")), MinimumTrials(25)],
                   require_complete_crossing=False)
trials = pd.DataFrame(synthesize_trials(block, 1, CMSGen)[0])
rest = trials.iloc[1:]                  # without the first trial
display(pd.crosstab(rest["trial_before"], rest["congruency"]))
congruency congruent incongruent trial_before congruent 6 6 incongruent 6 6

The four combinations are equal, and that is by design: run the cell again and they stay equal.

docs.title: What else repeats?
docs.text:
Not in the design: does the ink colour, and so the response, repeat from the trial before? Count it in each of the four combinations.

trials["response_repeats"] = trials["colour"].eq(trials["colour"].shift())
rest = trials.iloc[1:]
display(pd.crosstab([rest["trial_before"], rest["congruency"]], rest["response_repeats"]))
response_repeats False True trial_before congruency congruent congruent 4 2 incongruent 2 4 incongruent congruent 5 1 incongruent 4 2

Check. Is the response repeat equal across the four combinations? If not, the alternative explanation is still open. Whatever is not in the crossing is left to chance: run the block cell again and see which counts change.

Try. Ask what it would take to forbid all repeats (Exclude on a transition factor for the colour), and what that does to the four combinations.

Next. Step 3 goes from the trial before to the whole block: mostly congruent and mostly incongruent blocks.

docs.title: Step 3. Adaptation
docs.text: · notebook · script

docs.title: The experiment
docs.text: A block from the design built on this page. Press play, or step through it.

docs.title: With your assistant
docs.text: Now I want to test whether people adapt to the context. I want blocks in which most trials are congruent and blocks in which most are incongruent, and compare the congruency effect between them. What is the hypothesis, and what should I watch out for?

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
So far. Step 1 chose how many copies of each pair a block holds: 2 of each congruent pair, 1 of each incongruent pair. This step turns that choice into the manipulation.

The question. Do people adjust to how frequent conflict is?

Prediction. The congruency effect is smaller in mostly incongruent blocks than in mostly congruent blocks.

The alternative to rule out. In a mostly congruent block the word predicts the ink, so people can simply learn to follow the word.

The analysis. The congruency effect in mostly congruent blocks against the congruency effect in mostly incongruent blocks.

docs.title: As in step 1
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
from sweetpea import (Factor, DerivedLevel, WithinTrial, Transition, Exclude, MinimumTrials,
                      CrossBlock, synthesize_trials, CMSGen)

colours = ["red", "green", "blue"]

# regular factors: set freely on every trial
colour = Factor("colour", colours)      # the ink
word = Factor("word", colours)          # what the word says

# a derived factor: it follows from colour and word on the same trial
def same(colour, word):
    return colour == word


def different(colour, word):
    return colour != word


congruency = Factor("congruency", [
    DerivedLevel("congruent", WithinTrial(same, [colour, word])),
    DerivedLevel("incongruent", WithinTrial(different, [colour, word])),
])

def pairs_with_copies(congruent_copies, incongruent_copies):
    """Two helper factors that make every congruent pair occur `congruent_copies` times
    and every incongruent pair `incongruent_copies` times."""
    copy = Factor("copy", [str(n) for n in range(1, max(congruent_copies, incongruent_copies) + 1)])

    def too_many(copy, colour, word):
        return int(copy) > (congruent_copies if colour == word else incongruent_copies)

    def wanted(copy, colour, word):
        return not too_many(copy, colour, word)

    extra_copy = Factor("extra_copy", [
        DerivedLevel("too many", WithinTrial(too_many, [copy, colour, word])),
        DerivedLevel("wanted", WithinTrial(wanted, [copy, colour, word])),
    ])
    return copy, extra_copy

docs.title: New: two kinds of block
docs.text:
The number of copies sets the proportion. 6 copies of each congruent pair and 1 of each incongruent pair is 18 of 24 trials congruent; 2 and 3 copies is 6 of 24.

COPIES = {"mostly congruent": (6, 1), "mostly incongruent": (2, 3)}     # copies of each (congruent, incongruent) pair


def block(context):
    copy, extra_copy = pairs_with_copies(*COPIES[context])
    return CrossBlock(design=[colour, word, congruency, copy, extra_copy],
                      crossing=[colour, word, copy],
                      constraints=[Exclude((extra_copy, "too many"))],
                      require_complete_crossing=False)

docs.title: A session of four blocks
docs.text:
Each block is generated on its own and gets its context as a column.

blocks = []
for number, context in enumerate(["mostly congruent", "mostly incongruent", "mostly incongruent", "mostly congruent"], start=1):
    trials = pd.DataFrame(synthesize_trials(block(context), 1, CMSGen)[0])
    trials.insert(0, "context", context)
    trials.insert(0, "block", number)
    blocks.append(trials)
session = pd.concat(blocks, ignore_index=True)
display(pd.crosstab(session["context"], session["congruency"]))
congruency congruent incongruent context mostly congruent 36 12 mostly incongruent 12 36

docs.title: How well does the word tell the ink?
docs.text:
For each word, the share of trials on which it is shown in its own colour. That number is the alternative explanation.

session["word_is_ink"] = session["word"] == session["colour"]
display(session.groupby(["context", "word"])["word_is_ink"].mean().round(2).unstack())
word blue green red context mostly congruent 0.75 0.75 0.75 mostly incongruent 0.25 0.25 0.25

Check. Are the proportions what was asked for? How many incongruent trials does a mostly congruent block have: is that enough to measure the effect there? A word is in its own colour on 75% of the trials in one context and 25% in the other: how could learning and control be told apart?

Try. Change the copies to (4, 1) and (1, 2). What are the proportions and the block lengths now?

Next. Step 4 asks whether this adjustment has a price when the task changes.

docs.title: Step 4. Transfer
docs.text: · notebook · script

docs.title: The experiment
docs.text: A block from the design built on this page. Press play, or step through it.

docs.title: With your assistant
docs.text: Last question: does the adaptation transfer to another task? I want mini-blocks that are mostly congruent or mostly incongruent, and each mini-block is either colour naming or word reading. I want the switch cost between mini-blocks: word reading after colour naming against word reading after word reading, compared between the two contexts. I take word reading because it has almost no congruency effect. What is the hypothesis, and can nested blocks keep everything counterbalanced, also at the border between two mini-blocks: which context and which task came before?

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
So far. Step 2 made the trial before a factor. Step 3 made blocks that are mostly congruent or mostly incongruent, generated one by one. This step uses both ideas one level up: the mini-block is the unit, and the whole session is one design.

The question. Does adapting to frequent conflict make it harder to change the task?

Prediction if it is one control setting. Where conflict is frequent the current task is shielded more, so a change of task costs more: the switch cost is larger in the mostly incongruent context.

Why word reading. The switch cost is taken on word-reading mini-blocks. Word reading has almost no congruency effect, so the proportion itself hardly touches the trials the cost is measured on.

The analysis. Switch cost = response time in word-reading mini-blocks that follow colour naming (switch) minus response time in word-reading mini-blocks that follow word reading (repeat). Compare it between the two contexts.

docs.title: As before, plus the task and the context
docs.text:
Both are regular factors. Neither changes from trial to trial: each is held for a whole mini-block.

import pandas as pd
from sweetpea import (Factor, DerivedLevel, WithinTrial, Transition, Exclude, MinimumTrials,
                      CrossBlock, synthesize_trials, CMSGen)

colours = ["red", "green", "blue"]

# regular factors: set freely on every trial
colour = Factor("colour", colours)      # the ink
word = Factor("word", colours)          # what the word says
from sweetpea import Nest, IterateGen

context = Factor("context", ["mostly congruent", "mostly incongruent"])  # new: held for a whole mini-block
task = Factor("task", ["name the colour", "read the word"])              # new: held for a whole mini-block

docs.title: New: what happens at the border between two mini-blocks?
docs.text:
Two transition factors, as in step 2. Here they will look back one mini-block, not one trial: does the task change, and which context came before?

def task_repeats(task):
    return task[0] == task[-1]


def task_switches(task):
    return task[0] != task[-1]


task_transition = Factor("task_transition", [
    DerivedLevel("repeat", Transition(task_repeats, [task])),
    DerivedLevel("switch", Transition(task_switches, [task])),
])


def after_mostly_congruent(context):
    return context[-1] == "mostly congruent"


def after_mostly_incongruent(context):
    return context[-1] == "mostly incongruent"


context_before = Factor("context_before", [
    DerivedLevel("mostly congruent", Transition(after_mostly_congruent, [context])),
    DerivedLevel("mostly incongruent", Transition(after_mostly_incongruent, [context])),
])

docs.title: New: what the context makes frequent
docs.text:
A weight makes a level more frequent: the third argument of a level, and 3 to 1 is three quarters. But a level has one weight, and here the proportion depends on the context. SweetPea has no weight that depends on another factor. So the weight sits on a helper factor that says whether a trial is the kind its context makes frequent: congruent in a mostly congruent mini-block, incongruent in a mostly incongruent one.

def frequent_here(colour, word, context):
    congruent = colour == word
    return congruent == (context == "mostly congruent")


def rare_here(colour, word, context):
    return not frequent_here(colour, word, context)


frequency = Factor("frequency", [
    DerivedLevel("frequent", WithinTrial(frequent_here, [colour, word, context]), 3),
    DerivedLevel("rare", WithinTrial(rare_here, [colour, word, context]), 1),
])

docs.title: New: a block inside a block
docs.text:
Two blocks, each with its own crossing:

  • within a mini-block: the frequency crossed with the ink colour, 12 trials;
  • between mini-blocks: the context, the context before, the task and the task transition. That is every kind of border, 16 mini-blocks, plus a first one that has no mini-block before it.

Nest puts the first inside the second: every combination of the outer block is held for one whole mini-block.

mini_block = CrossBlock(design=[colour, word, frequency, context],
                        crossing=[frequency, colour],
                        constraints=[])
between_mini_blocks = CrossBlock(design=[context, context_before, task, task_transition],
                                 crossing=[context, context_before, task, task_transition],
                                 constraints=[])
block = Nest(outer_block=between_mini_blocks, inner_block=mini_block, alignment="post preamble")
session = pd.DataFrame(synthesize_trials(block, 1, IterateGen)[0])       # 204 trials: too long for CMSGen

# columns for counting
session["congruency"] = ["congruent" if colour == word else "incongruent"
                         for colour, word in zip(session["colour"], session["word"])]
session.insert(0, "block", session.index // 12 + 1)
overview = session.groupby("block")[["context_before", "context", "task", "task_transition"]].first()
overview["congruent trials"] = session.groupby("block")["congruency"].apply(lambda c: (c == "congruent").sum())
display(overview)

docs.title: What is not in the design?
docs.text:
The two trials at the border themselves: the last trial of one mini-block and the first trial of the next. Count them for the mini-blocks where the task switches.

first = session.groupby("block")["congruency"].first().rename("first trial after the border")
last_before = session.groupby("block")["congruency"].last().shift().rename("last trial before the border")
switches = mini_blocks[mini_blocks["task_transition"] == "switch"].index
display(pd.crosstab(last_before[switches], first[switches]))
first trial after the border congruent incongruent last trial before the border congruent 3 3 incongruent 2 0

Check. Both crossings are exact, and every kind of border occurs once. What is thin? Each kind of border is one mini-block of 12 trials; more need several sequences. The two trials at the border are left to chance: is that acceptable, or should the first trial of a mini-block be pinned?

The sampler. CMSGen did not finish this design in five minutes. IterateGen takes a few seconds, but it does not draw at random among all possible sequences: it returns the solutions in the order the solver finds them. Look at the order of the trials before you use it.

Try. Take context_before out of the outer block. How many mini-blocks are left, and does CMSGen work again?

The idea. Each question added a factor, and each factor multiplies the design. Nesting keeps both levels counterbalanced at once. What it leaves open is still a choice, and which choice is acceptable depends on what you compare.
